傳統風鳴琴多為木製共鳴箱，配有音板與音孔，兩座琴橋上張弦；家用型常見十至十二條腸: A traditional aeolian harp is mostly a wooden soundbox with a soundboard and soundholes, with strings stretched over two bridges; the domestic type usually has ten to twelve gut strings, and the material and thickness of the strings can vary. Large or outdoor pieces mostly use a metal frame or a metal resonator, and there are even sound sculptures made of metal on rooftops and hillsides, with metal discs used to help project the sound. The source does not state what the bridges and soundholes are made of.
實際聆聽多來自風吹動琴弦的隨機發聲，常見於家居窗邊、庭園裝飾、屋頂與山丘上的金屬: Most actual listening comes from the random sound of the wind moving the strings, common at a window at home, as garden decoration, in metal sound sculptures on rooftops and hillsides, and on the coasts of Denmark, Germany and Sweden; because no one plays it, this is chance music. In classical music, too, the organ has an 'aeolian harp' stop imitating its timbre, and Chopin's Étude in A flat major, Op. 25 No. 1, and Lyapunov's Études d'exécution transcendante, Op. 11 No. 9, are also named after the aeolian harp or imitate it.
無須持琴或撥弦。將風鳴琴置於微開窗邊或其他通風處，使風吹過張緊於兩座琴橋上的弦。: No holding or plucking is needed. Set the aeolian harp at a slightly open window or in another place with a draught, so that the wind blows across the strings stretched between the two bridges. The strings can all be tuned to the same pitch, or tuned to different pitches; when the wind speed changes you get different overtones and different dynamics. For a start, check that the strings are taut and the body secure, then choose a spot with a steady wind direction and watch how the wind sets the strings vibrating.

風鳴琴以風撥弦的原理自古已知，器物亦見於中國、衣索比亞、希臘、印度、印尼與美拉尼: The principle of the aeolian harp, strings plucked by the wind, has been known since ancient times, and such instruments are found in China, Ethiopia, Greece, India, Indonesia and Melanesia. In 1650 and 1673 Athanasius Kircher described the instrument in his writings. In the Romantic period it became a household instrument and it is still made by hand; today there are also metal sound sculptures on rooftops and on windy hillsides. In 1915 Lord Rayleigh explained its wind-driven vibration in a paper.
風鳴琴是僅以風發聲的弦鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs 編號 314.1: The aeolian harp is a chordophone sounded by the wind alone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 314.122. Traditionally it is a wooden soundbox with a soundboard, with strings stretched lengthwise between two bridges, often set at a slightly open window to let the wind blow across the strings; modern versions also use metal frames or large sound sculptures. It needs no one to pluck it: the wind makes the strings produce overtones, and it is common in the home, at windows, as garden decoration, and on European coasts, rooftops and windy gaps.
風鳴琴由風吹過張緊弦線產生週期性渦流而振動，只發出泛音，常見三度、八度、十二度泛: The aeolian harp is set vibrating by the periodic eddies the wind makes as it passes the taut strings; it gives only overtones — thirds, octaves and twelfths are common — and never the fundamental. Its timbre is therefore described as faint and airy, swelling and fading with the strength of the wind. Volume and pitch depend on the length, thickness and material of the strings, on the soundbox and on the direction of the wind; the harp can be set in a window or a draught, or given a wind funnel or metal discs to reinforce the sound. Unlike wind chimes it is not struck; unlike ordinary chordophones it does not produce a fundamental by plucking but drives overtones with the wind.
